graders: claude-haiku-5-5 (standalone CLI, project settings skipped), one book per run; inputs: captions with authored times, scene headers and the contact sheets of every chapter
note: Round 2 visual polish (Claude Haiku 5.5), final: all 487 book chapters and the 223 shared explainer scenes re-framed for layout and clarity. Captions, holds and every timing expression match the pre-polish commit exactly, in every file (checked by generator-free audit against f6a1c262^). Layout problems 6,473 -> 773 across 712 chapters; five chapters were restored to their original timing and carry 73 of the remaining problems. Graded on the same inputs as the baseline.

notes.accuracy: The ch3 bars end with the per-entry cost at 2^8.6 lookups against an 8-bit budget, and the red bar still runs past the green one, yet the chapter is titled "Making the bridge pay" and never says why the remaining 0.6 bits are acceptable. The ch1 and ch2 claims (256 texts, nine guessed bytes, scale and shift, canonical frame) match what the diagrams show.
notes.depth: Ch3 gives real numbers: about 19 bits naive, 8.6 bits after the techniques, a 2^89.3 to 2^91.4 time range, and 2^105 data. Ch2 names the two fingerprints but shows no formula beyond G = αD + β, and the power-sum ratio is only described in words.
notes.clarity: The arc is easy to follow, but the notation (⊕, S⁻¹, αD+β) is never explained on screen, and the captions are long and dense for a newcomer. The chip labels and checklist text are very small in the contact sheets.
notes.story: Ch1 plants the question of whether one more byte can vanish, ch2 answers it with the orbit bridge, and ch3 asks whether the bridge pays off in practice. Nothing closes the book with a memorable line; it ends on a result figure.
notes.visual: Most frames are legible and uncluttered, and the ch3 final frame is clean. Minor problems: scatter points sit on or past the bottom edge of the offline panel in ch2 (about 9–15 s and 40–43 s), the struck-through "unknown key byte" chip and the "×1/256" label are tiny and low-contrast, and ch1's R5/R6 chips fade almost to invisible.
notes.sync: Caption text and visual changes line up on paper: the k-chips appear with the nine-guess caption, the canonical frame appears with the fingerprint-moving-frame caption, and the crossed-out byte appears with the ninth-byte caption. Motion and timing cannot be seen from stills, so this stays within the 6.5–7.5 range.
notes.sound: Counting words against the authored caption durations gives roughly 200–310 wpm, well above the 110–170 target: ch1 caption 1 is about 196 wpm, ch2 caption 0 about 284 wpm, and ch3 caption 7 about 310 wpm. Expanded identifiers ("two to the one hundred five") are handled well, but the pace is a clear problem. I could not hear the audio, so this is judged from the script and the timings.
notes.curiosity: The ch3 result of 2^89.3 to 2^91.4 still below 2^128 is a sharp hook, and the orbit-frame idea makes the reader want to see the code. The ch2 bridge metaphor sticks well.

notes.accuracy: The on-screen identity in chapter 2 (t≈3s–40s) reads as a chain χ(a,b;c,d) = [(a+c)(b+d)]/[(a+d)(b+c)]·χ(a,b;c,d) = (a+d)(b+c)(a+c)(b+d), whose final product does not follow from the step before it; at sheet resolution this looks like a real error. Chapter 3's 'drop rate matches the derived probability' is asserted in narration but no number or derived value appears on screen, so it cannot be traced.
notes.depth: Chapter 2 gives the actual mechanism (translation and inversion cancelling in the ratio, and the round-by-round 'one χ / four χ / mixed' progression) and chapter 3 gives a real control experiment. However, no numbers appear anywhere, the round-3 rotation defect is never described, and 'meet-in-the-middle' and 'field-rank' are used without explanation.
notes.clarity: Frames are mostly simple and the scene sequence is easy to follow. The narration, however, is dense (about 170–250 words per minute by caption text) and several technical terms are undefined for a newcomer, so the beats are hard to absorb.
notes.story: The arc is strong: chapter 1 sets an impossible brief, chapter 2 finds the surviving object, and chapter 3 withdraws a false discovery before a narrower payoff. The 'one remaining object' from chapter 1 is paid off in chapter 3's 'Möbius Bridge · cross-ratio · what survives' node, and the closing caption lands on a concrete, memorable result.
notes.visual: The kicker label 'FINDING THE BRIDGE · n' collides with the title in all three chapters. Candidate labels in the ghosted state (ch1) and the annotations and ledger text (ch2 round labels, ch3 ledger and the 'meet-in-the-middle consumes the invariant' line) are very small and low contrast. Chapter 1's opening frames are mostly empty space around a single box, and the chapter 2 stage changes size and position between frames.
notes.sync: Cues line up with captions where I could check: chapter 1's lens chips appear at the 'five lenses' caption, chapter 2's 'round 1 / round 2 / round 3' chips follow the propagation caption, and chapter 3's control curve and the 'withdrawn' ledger flip coincide with the control caption. Motion and exact landing points cannot be seen from stills, so this stays in the 6.5–7.5 band.
notes.sound: By caption text, narration pace runs about 145–260 wpm, with most captions above the 170 wpm ceiling (chapter 2 caption 6 is about 259 wpm; chapter 1 captions 1 and 5 are about 180–210). That is a clear problem, so the score drops below the usual band. 'Möbius' and 'χ' are pronunciation risks, and the formula is never narrated. Music and mix cannot be judged.
notes.curiosity: The chapter 3 reveal that 'the apparent discovery is withdrawn' and the reframing of the book as 'honest dead ends' leave a sharp question about why the cross-ratio survives when the other candidates fail. The final caption makes it clear the reader will want to look at the code.

notes.accuracy: The routing logic is right: last matching pattern wins, /db/** and /migrations/** don't match a file under prisma/migrations, and **/*.sql does. Three claims are unverified or overstated: that GitHub ignores text after an inline hash, that GitHub resolves CODEOWNERS from the base branch for PRs, and that Codex supports project-scoped agents in this TOML form. Chapter 2 also says edit and bash are denied 'by default' when the file sets them explicitly.
notes.depth: The chapters explain mechanisms (file-order matching, base versus head SHA, adapter normalization, the ruleset's single required check) with a concrete worked example that has real numbers and a safe migration sequence. Edge cases are thin: there is no discussion of unmatched files, a missing agent definition, or pattern anchoring rules.
notes.clarity: Captions define harness and agent before use, and the diagrams track the narration closely. Some captions are dense, and 'foobar review' is a placeholder name sitting next to a real harness (OpenCode), which may confuse a newcomer.
notes.story: The arc runs routing, then harnesses, then trust boundary, then worked example, then merge gate, and the closer 'one check, additive, growable' lands. The 'codex/migration-safety-review' entry in chapter 1 is planted but never paid off.
notes.visual: Frames are legible and uncluttered with a consistent palette and clean end cards. Clipping and overlap problems recur: header labels are cut by timestamp badges, the 'no effect' label sits on the trust-boundary line, and the end card covers the shared-interface box in chapter 2.
notes.sync: Caption midpoints line up with the tile times in every chapter, and each highlight appears when its caption names it. One mismatch: chapter 4 at t=55.2 shows the rerun already finished while the caption still says the agents are starting. Judged from the timing data only, so kept in range.
notes.sound: The narration pace looks too fast if the narration fills each caption's authored duration: about 25 words in 6.4 to 6.6 seconds is roughly 230 wpm, against a 110-170 target. Identifiers are spoken well ('dot sql', 'hash mark', 'Codex, the package file reviewer'). Judged from the script and timing only, so this is a pace risk to check by listening.
notes.curiosity: The closing lines leave an open thread: a new agent joins the roster without touching the ruleset, and the 'two readers' idea of one line for both humans and workflows is memorable. The chapter 1 frame where one line serves two readers is the sharpest hook.

issues.problem: Narration pace looks well above 170 wpm if the narration fills each caption's dur, for example about 26 words in 6.6 s (~236 wpm) and about 23 words in 7.2 s (~190 wpm); this pattern repeats in every chapter.

notes.accuracy: The depth colormap formula, the seven-segment color path, and the _grid_positions arithmetic (row 5.125, col 12.5 gives coarse cell (1,3)) check out against the cited code. Ch3's p_start = min(65, 61−4) = 57 and the 8-position shift are consistent with the 49-frame sink-plus-history budget. The image token count is wrong on screen: the label says 398 tokens for a 15×26 grid, which is 390, and the caption repeats 398. The (D+N)/2 averaging step is not visibly backed by the materials.
notes.depth: Ch2 shows real mechanism: the detached Z1 stop, the teacher-forcing pass with recomputed history K/V, and the blockwise mask versus call-order floating-point divergence, which is labeled schematic with no measured divergence. Ch3 works through the sink-five, recent-44 budget and the rotary-position trim. An expert would respect this, though much of it stays schematic.

notes.accuracy: The protocol claims match the cited spec: 201 on PUT, Stream-Up-To-Date, held-open long-poll with empty answers, SSE control events carrying streamNextOffset, Stream-Closed, fork headers, and zombie fencing by epoch. notes.accuracy: The chain of claims (mask ROM, then bootloader, then OTA selection, then per-core FreeRTOS, then UART FIFO, ISR, queue, and the Wi-Fi/netif/driver stack) matches the esp-idf names shown on screen. notes.accuracy: The arithmetic checks out: 0.95^20 is about 0.358, 45.16 − 31.47 = 13.69, 45.16 − 3.15 = 42.01, and the context budget (60+30+400 = 490 tokens per step, 128k window) lands at step 258. Chapter 5's Bayes precision (0.6·0.98 / (0.6·0.98 + 0.4·0.1) ≈ 93.6%) is correct, but the sheet's measured 93.3% from 2,938 + 210 counts doesn't reconcile cleanly with a 10% slip rate on 2,000 false claims (200, not 210).
notes.depth: Chapters 3 and 4 give real mechanisms: quadratic re-reading cost against linear retrieval cost, the compounding p^n survival curve with a Monte Carlo check, and a poisoned-observation case. Chapter 5 adds the critic's conditional-precision math. The numbers are toy-scale, though, and the 'accepted-claim precision' and 'Bayes' terms are never unpacked for a non-expert.
notes.clarity: Captions are short and speakable, and the chapter 1 loop is easy to follow. Terms like 'precision', 'base rate' and 'Bayes' appear in chapter 5 without a definition beat, and the on-screen formulas (cost(n) = Σ(s+k·i)…) are too dense to follow for a newcomer.
notes.story: The chapter 1 question (which rover went farther) is paid off by the chapter 1 answer, and chapter 1's promise that 'the rest of this book is what breaks' is carried through chapters 2 to 4. Chapter 5 closes the series arc with the line 'cheap belief for bad news, expensive belief for good news', which is a memorable close. The chapter 2 and 4 bridges to the other books are clear.
notes.visual: The stage frames are mostly clean, with legible captions and a consistent dark palette. Several frames are near-empty or mid-fade (chapter 1 at 3.3s, chapter 3 at 3.3s, chapter 5 at 47s), the chapter 2 tree row labels and the chapter 4 'failure three' card text are very small, and the chapter 2 tree nodes crowd together at 44s. notes.accuracy: Most numbers check out against the frames: 1.27 street width, 3 support vectors, 9 leave-one-out mistakes, 1/60 and 221 to 36 to 35 on the charts. Four claims contradict what is on screen: chapter 2's root says 98 points while the children sum to 90, chapter 3 says a factor of thirty while its panel reads 1/28, chapter 3 says zero wrong while the ensemble shows 1/60, and chapter 5 says seven hundred to seventy seven while the bar shows 221 to 35.
notes.depth: Strong mechanisms for a newcomer book: entropy and information gain with worked gains (0.38, 0.62), leave-one-out validation, the distance-contrast collapse by dimension, variance cut by averaging, AdaBoost reweighting, the kernel trick on XOR, and k-means' fixed-k and equal-spread assumptions with the GMM fix. Edge cases such as the variance-independence caveat and the stump's inability to separate the clouds are present.
notes.clarity: Captions are short, one idea per beat, and define terms before use (leaf, gain, margin, support vector, kernel). Sentences are speakable, and each chapter's on-screen labels are plain.
notes.story: Each chapter opens by planting a question (which line to trust, which question to ask, how to stop the tree) and pays it off, and the chapter 5 closer ties all five chapters together. The closing lines ('business model of the random forest', 'one of them in disguise') give each chapter a memorable end.
notes.visual: Most frames are clean and high-contrast, with consistent palette, legible charts, and clean ending cards. The main defect is that the chapter 2 and chapter 4 formulas render twice on top of each other in the top corner, so the text looks garbled. notes.curiosity: Each chapter ends on a sharp mental model: distance collapse in high dimensions, the staircase signature of trees, averaging as variance division, the widest street carried by three points, and k-means as a special case of the mixture. These make the reader want to open the code, though some endings are cut short by the closing card.

notes.accuracy: The core arithmetic holds: 2+2+8+4 = 16 bytes per parameter, 98 GiB, 6.57B parameters, the ZeRO figures 98/34/23/12, the pipeline bubbles 75/27.3/8.6%, and the ring totals 18.4 GB and 36.7 GB. Several claims are wrong or inconsistent, though: the ch2 caption says naive all-to-all ships 'thirty seven gigabytes per gigabyte' where the ledger implies 3x, the ch1 frame labels 'training state: 60.6 GiB' over bars that sum to about 73.4, and the ch5 worst-expert load is shown as 1.27x, drawn as 1361/1024 = 1.33x, and narrated as 'one point two'.
notes.depth: Real mechanisms are shown: the seeded ring all-reduce with step-by-step chunk sums, a 2x4 matrix split with the exchange at the seam, the pipeline schedule at 1, 8 and 32 microbatches, and a top-2 routing simulation with 8192 assignments. The trade-offs are named (bandwidth for memory, bubbles versus per-layer chatter, load imbalance) and the book admits that activations are left out. A practitioner would respect the numbers.
notes.clarity: The captions are short and speakable, and each chapter builds one idea on the last, from the tower to the cut to the sharding to the experts. Terms like 'bubble', 'microbatch' and 'all-reduce' are introduced with a visual before the jargon piles up. Some frames carry dense number labels, so a newcomer may need to pause to read them.
notes.story: The chapter-1 question, how to split the tower, is answered across chapters 2 to 5 and the end cards carry the thread. The chapter closers 'pick your tax' and 'choosing which bill to pay' tie the series together well. The arc is tidy and the closing line is memorable.
notes.visual: The pipeline grids and the ZeRO bars are clean and readable at a glance, and the end cards are clean. Several problems are visible: an unlabeled grey staircase shape sits beside the bars in every ch4 frame, the optimizer label in ch1 at t=21.6 is low-contrast, the ch3 matrix numbers are tiny with faint text on grey tiles, and the ch2/ch4 end-card transitions show ghosted chart residue behind the title card. The ch5 t= timestamp also overlaps a parameter box at t=40.1.
notes.sync: No narration cue times were authored for any chapter (every caption list reads none), so the on-screen captions cannot be checked against narration timing. The captions and the visuals agree within each frame. Scored in the 6.5-7.5 band as instructed, without a watched playback.
notes.sound: Narration audio was not provided and the captions carry no narration timing. Pace and pronunciation cannot be judged. Scored in the 6.5-7.5 band as instructed.

notes.accuracy: The bloom-filter math checks out: 46% at n=5 and 10.0% FPR, 63% and 25.3% at n=8. The ch6 counter goes 41 to 42 after an alice +1 that the batch run at t=30.9 already included, so the delta is counted twice. notes.clarity: Terms are defined before use, for example 'bit array' and 'arc', and most captions are short enough to follow. The ch1 mod-N to ring to virtual-node progression is easy to follow. Some Raft frames rely on tiny log squares and labels that a newcomer has to squint at.

notes.accuracy: The chapters are well sourced in places (SWE-bench Verified's 38.3% underspecified and 61.1% unfair-tests figures, HLE's 2,500 questions and $500k prizes, the 27 Leaderboard Illusion variants). But on-screen numbers contradict captions in ch2 and ch4, the ch2 leaderboard figures (92.1/91.4/90.8) are unlabeled as illustrative, and the ch4 'mid-2026 ~45-53%' figure has no source.
notes.depth: The chapters show real mechanisms: a sigmoid ability-to-score curve, a sieve over 400 items, the pool-refresh gap collapsing from 13.6 to about 0.5 points, a fixed-vs-rolling pool simulation, and six named design rules. An expert would respect the simulation and the 160-item toy model, though the sieve and leaderboard numbers are shallow.
notes.clarity: Captions are speakable and define terms before use (saturation as 'the instrument goes deaf', leakage as 'a test becomes a memory test'). Each chapter carries one idea per beat, and the chart labels are short enough to follow with the narration.
notes.story: The arc runs from the dying benchmarks (ch1) to three deaths (ch2), a real-world case (ch3), a design fix (ch4) and a six-rule checklist (ch5). The 'Book seventeen' question is planted in ch1 and paid off in ch5, and the closing line 'the eval that lasts is the one that stays harder to game than the task is to solve' is memorable.
notes.visual: The pictures carry the ideas well (the dots drifting from public test set into the crawl, the sieve culling, the fixed pool running away from true skill). Labels are often tiny at this scale, labels sit on lines (SuperGLUE, 'gap 1.0 pts'), and several end cards sit over faded charts, which muddies the last frames.
notes.sync: No caption start or duration values were supplied (the narration list is empty), so I can only check that tile times match the caption text on screen. Those match, but I could not see motion or confirm cue timing, so this stays in the 6.5-7.5 band.
notes.sound: Captions are about 6 seconds apart and carry 27-37 words each, which implies roughly 270-370 wpm if the narration fills each window, well above the 110-170 target. Identifiers are spelled for the ear ('M M L U', 'G P T', 'H L E', 'Open A I'), but the pace is the problem. Caption durations were not provided, so this is an inference from tile spacing.
notes.curiosity: The closing question 'will the benchmark still measure anything in two years?' and the ch4 'a filter has a half-life' idea leave a sharp new mental model. Ch3 also makes you want to open the SWE-bench repo and check the test-suite claims.

notes.accuracy: The core claims hold up: 3.74 fresh error against 0.000 leaked, 0.025/0.031 for the honest model, ECE 0.239 to 0.041, and 47% of 2000 reruns. Several figures disagree across chapters or with their own captions: ch5 shows 'truth 0.005' where ch2 says 0.003, ch3 says 'about thirty' while the screen shows ÷38.7, and ch4 says 'nineteen of every twenty' while its screen shows a 7.1% loss rate. The ch2 curves are stylized shapes, which the 'recorded live' framing does not disclose.
notes.depth: Each chapter gives a concrete mechanism and a number: 12 knobs interpolating 12 points, a 24.8-weight cliff, a sqrt(n) noise argument, and a three-station attack gauntlet. Temperature scaling and the reliability diagram get only one pass, and the trade-offs of the gauntlet are not explored, so it reads more like a strong overview than expert depth.
notes.clarity: Terms are introduced on screen before they are used, including 'leaked', 'proxy', 'reliability diagram' and 'expected calibration error'. The captions are long, though, often 25 to 40 words per card, which hurts the one-idea-per-beat rule and speakability.
notes.story: The five chapters build a clear arc: leaked questions, then gamed proxies, then overconfidence, then noisy gains, then the gauntlet. The 'better, or lucky?' question is answered in ch4, the ch1 numbers reappear as evidence in ch5, and the closing line 'the honest evaluation is the one that wants to catch you' lands well.
notes.visual: Most frames are legible and the diagrams carry their ideas, but several problems recur. Curves cross labels in ch2, the reliability-diagram axes in ch3 are tiny, the n=10,000 histograms in ch4 collapse into thin spikes, and the stamps in ch5 overhang panel borders while panel positions shift between frames. In ch1 the polynomial tails run off the top and bottom of the stage, and the end cards sit over faded charts.
notes.sync: Within the frames shown, motion and captions agree: the ch2 curve climbs as its caption describes, and the ch5 station panels appear as they are named. The sheets carry no narration cue times, so true audio sync cannot be checked here.
notes.sound: Caption spacing in the sheets is about 6 seconds per card, and many cards carry 25 to 35 words, which implies roughly 250 to 340 wpm if the narration tracks the captions, well above the 110 to 170 target. This is inferred from spacing, not heard. Identifiers such as 'ECE' and 'T*' appear only on screen and their pronunciation is not handled in the captions.
notes.curiosity: The ch4 card 'a coin flip wearing a lab coat' and the ch2 line that the benchmark 'cannot see its own failure' leave a sharp mental model. The ch5 line 'a metric that has never been attacked is not evidence yet' makes the reader want to try the gauntlet on code.

notes.accuracy: Chapter 4's narration says task A holds at zero point one and task B at zero point zero six with replay, but the on-screen table reads 0.009 and 0.006, a tenfold mismatch on the chapter's headline result. notes.depth: Chapter 1 gives rank, storage and error trade-offs with correct arithmetic (32, 64, 128 numbers against 256; 65,536 against 16,777,216), and chapter 3 gives the int8 versus int4 error ratio and the outlier scale penalty. notes.clarity: The flow is easy to follow, with one idea per chapter and plain-language glosses like 'the directions of the update, by strength'. Terms such as logits, softmax, loss, MLP and Jacobi sweeps appear without definition, and chapter 3's captions pack several numbers into one sentence.
notes.story: There is a clear arc: chapter 1 plants 'how much structure is hiding in there?' and answers it, chapter 2 turns the dark knowledge into a payoff, chapter 3 sets up the outlier trap and its bargain, and chapter 4 ends on 'unless the old one keeps voting'. The closing line 'learn only the nudge' pays off chapter 1's 'nudges' opening.

notes.curiosity: The chapters end on sharp questions and mental models: why the update lives in a thin slice of weight space, why a teacher's wrong answers carry information, why one outlier triples the error, and whether the shared neurons are voting. Each one makes the viewer want to open the code.

notes.accuracy: The arithmetic checks out: 192 KiB per token × 128k = 24 GiB, f=1/8 gives 3 GiB, and 18 × 3 GiB fits in the 56 GiB left after the 24 GiB of weights. The overclaims are the uncited 'Frontier models stopped choosing' thesis, the 'card is full' caption over a frame showing 19 GiB free, and the 'one eighth the bytes' payoff, which ignores the weight reads.
notes.depth: Mechanisms and numbers are real: the KV-versus-state recall error curves, the softmax spotlight versus linear-memory leakage, the 300-trial store-size sweep, the 40% versus 85% placement result, and the noise-halving argument (σ/√4). Trade-offs are thin, though. The book never says what the recurrent layers lose beyond the toy's needle and summary tasks.

notes.accuracy: Chapter 2's joint table, independent twin, H(sky)=0.88, H(umbrella)=0.89, joint 1.43 and I=0.35 all check out, as do Chapter 4's C=0.531, repeat-3 error 2.8% and repeat-5 error 0.86%, and Chapter 5's 190/163/120 bits and 14-symbol alphabet. Chapter 1's displayed letter percentages sum to 108%, and recomputing from them gives entropy of about 2.78 and a Huffman average of about 2.81, not the 2.771 and 2.800 shown. Chapter 3's 'true codebook' bars read 1.01 and 2.99 where the true lengths are 1 and 3.
notes.depth: Chapters 2 to 5 give real mechanisms and numbers: the block-failure probability at two or three flips, the rate-versus-error trade-off, KL as a asymmetric price rather than a distance, and the bigram cost per character. Chapter 1 stops at the Huffman-to-entropy gap and never says that block coding can close it, and no chapter covers a failure mode beyond the basic case. An expert would respect the numbers but would want one more edge case.
notes.clarity: The arc from fixed-width codes to Huffman to mutual information to KL to channel capacity to prediction is easy to follow, and each chapter opens with a plain-language problem. Entropy is used as a number in Chapter 1 before it is defined in words, and the dense formula strips (I(X;Y), D_KL, H(P,Q)) are heavy for a newcomer. The phrase 'the books do not balance' in Chapter 2 is an unclear metaphor.
notes.story: Each chapter ends with a bridge to the next ('Next we ask what one signal is worth in bits about another'; 'Next, what it costs when your probabilities are simply wrong'). Chapter 5 pays off the series by showing that the code lengths of Chapter 1 fall out of the predictor, and the closing line 'prediction turned out to be compression wearing a different hat' is worth remembering.

notes.accuracy: The core claims check out: the ten-to-eleven sort trace (median reported as 11, true 10), the 473 of 2,000 wrong lists (23.6%), the shrink to [2, 0, 100] at step 28, and the 11%, 3.7% and 2.3% violation rates all match their own arithmetic. The Chapter 1 'eight green' table contradicts itself: the last row reads median([8,2,9,4,6]) expect 4 with a green tick, but the true median is 6 and the buggy sort also returns 6. Chapter 4 shows 'space 26^6 = 389 million' on screen while the caption says three hundred nine million, and 26^6 is 308,915,776.
notes.depth: Real mechanisms are shown: string versus numeric sort, shrinking as a process, the coverage-guided corpus, and ECE per bucket. The chapters lean on toy models, though, and Chapter 5 gives only one aggregate calibration figure with no discussion of how it was measured.
notes.clarity: Terms are defined before use (metamorphic relation, shrinking, coverage, calibration), and the captions are short, speakable sentences. Chapter 2's property line is dense notation, but the caption restates it in words.
notes.story: The arc is clear: the oracle wall in Chapter 1, the property that replaces it in Chapter 2, relations in Chapter 3, guided search in Chapter 4, and the three AI families in Chapter 5. Chapter 1's 'ask where those eight expected values came from' is paid off, and each chapter ends by handing a question to the next.
notes.visual: Most frames are legible and the diagrams carry their ideas: the sorted list with its wrong median, the shrink ladder ending on the gold witness, the bar chart with its perfect-calibration line. Several frames have large empty stage areas early on (Chapter 1 at 3.2s and 8.8s, Chapter 3 at 3.4s), and the small labels in Chapter 4 and the chart tick labels in Chapter 5 are close to illegible at this size.
notes.sync: Narration cue times were not supplied (every chapter lists none), so I could not check sync against the words. The caption-to-frame progression on the sheets is plausible, so I score this from the materials only: 7.
notes.sound: Captions are short and mostly speakable, and the identifiers are written out in words (for example 'the median', 'the property'). I could not hear pace or pronunciation, so this stays in the 6.5-7.5 range.
notes.curiosity: The opening hook (eight green tests, a quarter of the space wrong) is sharp, and every chapter ends on a question that the next answers. Asking what can be asserted about a model itself is a strong closer.

issues.problem: The 'eight green examples' table shows median([8,2,9,4,6]) expect 4 with a green tick, but the true median is 6 and the buggy implementation also returns 6, so a green result is shown for a wrong expectation. The book's central demo contradicts itself.
issues.fix: Change the expected value in that row to 6 (and check the other rows) so the example shows 8/8 green for the right reason, or make the row visibly fail and rewrite the caption to match.

issues.problem: The on-screen space size reads '389 million' and '1 of 389 million', while the Chapter 1 caption and the Chapter 4 caption say three hundred nine million. 26^6 is 308,915,776, so the on-screen figure is wrong (or misread from a small tile).

notes.accuracy: Chapter 1's spoken numbers disagree with its own panel: the caption says A is six degrees away at cosine 0.995 and B is twenty-four degrees at 0.92, while the panel shows A at 0.997 (4 degrees) and B at 0.888 (27 degrees). Chapter 3 says the found node is 'provably the true nearest neighbor', which overclaims for an approximate index that was checked on one query.
notes.depth: The chapters carry real mechanisms: raw dot product versus cosine, the unit-circle identity, the N times d cost table with a 10 ms budget line, and HNSW layer counts with a 21-versus-60 comparison receipt. Missing are HNSW's build and search parameters and the recall trade-off, so an expert would still want the failure cases of the greedy walk.
notes.clarity: Terms are introduced before use (dot product, unit circle, layers) and the captions are short and speakable, with identifiers spelled out for the ear (seven hundred sixty eight dimensions, one hundred million). Chapter 2 mentions skip lists as known before the term is defined, and the cosine caption packs several numbers into one sentence.
notes.story: The arc is strong: the 'trap' planted in chapter 1 is paid off by the jaguar example in chapter 4, exhaustion in chapter 2 sets up HNSW in chapter 3, and the closing lines ('the right one to believe') land. Each chapter ends on a line that hands off to the next.
notes.visual: Most frames are clean and readable, with a clear before-and-after on the unit circle and a clear red failure state in chapter 4. Small clipping and clutter remain: the chapter 1 cosine panel runs to the frame edge, chapter 2's bar and formula text is very small, chapter 4's end cards show ghosted panels through them, and the chapter 4 cheetah label sits on top of its own ray.
notes.sync: Timing cannot be verified because every narration caption has no dur value, so the judgment rests on the cue times. Chapter 2's caption 'four hundred comparisons later' lands on a frame that reads 375 of 400, which suggests the counter lags the words slightly.
notes.sound: No narration durations were supplied, so words per minute cannot be measured and the audio cannot be heard. The scripts are speakable and the formula is expanded for the ear, but the chapter 1 numbers would be read aloud as mismatched against the screen.
notes.curiosity: Each chapter ends on a sharp hook: why a louder document wins, why the nearest neighbor is not the answer, why a few layers of express lanes make search fast, and what a jaguar query does to the answer. Viewers would want to read the index code afterward.

issues.problem: The narration says document A is six degrees away at cosine 0.995 and document B is twenty-four degrees away at 0.92, but the on-screen panel shows A at 0.997 (4 degrees) and B at 0.888 (27 degrees).

notes.story: The chapters connect: ch1 'you cannot sweet talk a test suite' is paid off in ch4 ('True — but you can memorize one'), ch2's open question 'can a gradient climb it' is answered, and ch3 ends with 'next chapter, we attack it'. The ch5 closing line 'build the check harder to game than the task is to solve' is a strong ending.

notes.accuracy: The mechanisms shown (origin as scheme+host+port, postMessage as the only channel, the origin guard, the 60s timeout) are concrete, but several claims are stated as absolute with no source on screen: 'exactly one sanctioned pinhole', 'the only bypass', 'the most adversarially-tested primitive on the web', and 'twenty five years'. The README quote in ch1 cannot be checked from these frames.
notes.depth: Ch3 shows real architecture (credentialless iframe, service worker, init/execute/result/console message list) and ch4 names the trade-offs (snapshot copies, async round trips, console relay). However, the cost is never quantified: no latency, copy-size or timeout numbers beyond '60s', and the edge cases are mostly listed in tables rather than explained.
notes.clarity: The ch1 and ch2 narrative is easy to follow, and the origin triple is defined before it is used. Ch3 and ch4 drop terms a newcomer will not know, such as credentialless, VFSSnapshot, syncFile and structured-clone, with no gloss on screen.
notes.story: The arc holds: ch1 raises the untrusted-code problem, ch2 introduces the browser wall, ch3 builds the cage, ch4 prices it, and ch5 generalizes it. The 'what does untrusted really cost' question from ch1 is paid off in ch4, and the ch5 closer ('an agent you cannot contain is an agent you cannot verify') is memorable.
notes.visual: The diagrams carry the ideas well in ch1 and ch2, and the closing cards are clean. But ch3 has the dashed same-origin wall running through the message-list labels, ch4 has a callout cut off by the caption bar, and ch5 has the chip row colliding with the table header. The timecode badge also covers the first letters of the chapter titles in ch1 to ch4, though this may be a sheet annotation rather than book content.
notes.sync: Narration cue data was not supplied (captions listed as none), so I cannot check cue times against the spoken lines. The burned-in captions do change on schedule with the diagram builds, so I can only rate sync provisionally.
notes.sound: The caption wording is speakable and spells out identifiers ('sixty seconds', 'node runtime'). Words per minute and music level cannot be measured from these materials, so this stays provisional.
notes.curiosity: Lines like 'isolation is the art of subtracting authority' and 'untrusted = someone else's interests, your authority' give a sharp new mental model. The ch4 closing question of why the unsafe path still ships makes the viewer want to open the code.

notes.accuracy: The binomial math checks out: 13 of 20 with p=0.55 and 1-(1-0.2)^16 ≈ 97% both match the frames. The published figures (Wang 2022 56.5% to 74% at 40 paths; Brown 2024 15.9% to 56% at 250 samples) are labelled as reported, but the chapter 3 claim about 'published process-supervision studies' is uncited, and the chapter 5 'roughly linear in log' claim rests on two-point cards.
notes.depth: The chapters give real mechanisms (the binomial lottery, the trap-answer vote, min-over-steps scoring, beam width against nodes expanded, and a compute-per-answer trade). The simulated judges are idealised, though: the verifier is perfect and the process judge reaches 99.9%, and the book only partly flags this. An expert would want the cost and failure modes of verifiers, not just the upside.
notes.clarity: Terms are defined before use: pass@N becomes 'a verifier can check each one', the PRM becomes 'min over the steps', and beam becomes 'keep the four best partial paths alive'. Each caption is mostly one idea, and the on-screen numbers match the spoken ones. Some chapter 5 captions are dense, and 'sixteen draws almost guarantee a winner' overstates a 97% chance.
notes.story: The chapters form a clear chain: sample, then vote and verify, then grade steps, then search, then scaling. Each one ends by setting up the next ('Next chapter: what more samples actually buy', 'which raises the next question', 'the last chapter asks the economic question'). The closing line 'compute per answer became a dial' pays off the opening 'buying more tickets'.
notes.visual: The frames are legible overall, with clean title cards and a clear 'trap wins 7 of 9 votes' moment. Several frames are weak: the chapter 1 dot strip is nearly invisible against the background, the chapter 2 opening stack is faint, and end cards sit over ghosted charts. Axis ticks, tree node labels and legends are tiny and low contrast, and the chapter 4 'fork 3' label is clipped at the frame edge.
notes.sync: Sync cannot be checked from stills, so this is judged from the frame times. Chapter 4 names the width-4 and width-16 results at 33.4s, but those points only appear around 39s. Chapter 3 narrates 99.9% at 128 samples while its process line ends at 16 samples (98.7%).
notes.sound: Audio cannot be heard, so this is judged from the caption text. The materials list no narration captions, yet every frame shows caption text, so the authored timing is unverified. Several captions carry 35 to 50 words in one 4 to 6 second window, which risks pace above 170 wpm. The end cards use 'pass@1' and 'p ∈ [0.05, 0.95]', which need expanding for the ear.
notes.curiosity: The hooks are sharp: 'one sample is a lottery ticket', 'the trap answer', 'luck and logic look identical from the outside', and 'the dial only works when something can check the answer'. Each chapter leaves a question open that makes you want to see the next one or look at the simulation code.

notes.accuracy: The demo numbers check out: the 10/100 and 0/25 counts, the 36 occlusion positions, the 0.25 quarter-drops and the 0.47/0.11 attention rows all match their frames. notes.depth: The book goes past an overview: it covers kernel weights, max-pool shift invariance, the hierarchy's corner template, attention over patches, and occlusion saliency with the 0.75 floor. It also names trade-offs, such as convolution's built-in locality versus a transformer's need for data. It stops short of edge cases like stride, padding, or what happens when the occluder is larger than a feature.
notes.clarity: Terms such as kernel, pooling, corner map and saliency are introduced before they are used, and each chapter carries one idea. The attention chapter is the weak spot: it says 'no trained weights' without explaining what attention scores mean in an untrained model, which a newcomer will stumble on.
notes.story: The arc runs from edges to pooling to hierarchy to attention to occlusion. The chapter 1 question 'what tiny patterns is this grid made of?' is paid off, and the chapter 5 'receipt' idea answers the chapter 1 framing. The closing line 'That is computer vision, end to end' lands cleanly.
notes.visual: Most frames are legible and uncluttered, and the stage-by-stage diagrams carry the idea. Several frames cost points: the chapter 5 formula box covers the bottom of the saliency grid and the score bar, the pooled and kernel numbers are very small, the chapter 3 'edges' labels float detached, and the final frames of chapters 3 and 5 fade to near-empty dim stages.

notes.accuracy: The Koa mechanics match the cited backing files: 404 default, status flip on body set, compose's 'next() called multiple times' guard, the resolved promise at i === length, and ctx.throw's expose flag. notes.depth: The chapters cover real mechanisms rather than an overview: the await suspension, the index guard, delegation through the request and response wrappers, and the catch-at-the-rim error path with headerSent. notes.story: The arc is clear: build the onion, then send a request through it, then errors. Planted questions pay off, with 'eight lines' and 'the last word' in chapter 3 answered in chapter 5, and the chapter 3 'error handling two chapters from now' promise is kept. The closing line in chapter 5 is memorable.

The ch2 'hold that thought' promise is interrupted by the deferral chapter before ch4 finally pays it, and the closing line 'precision is the lever' lands well.

notes.clarity: Each chapter introduces one idea per beat, and terms such as hot and cold experts, the router, and the registry are defined before the frames use them. The on-screen labels reinforce the narration, so a newcomer can follow the sequence.

notes.accuracy: The protocol details are largely right: secp256k1 with y²=x³+7, HKDF salt 'nip44-v2', 76 bytes split 32/12/32, the 99-byte minimum, calc_padded_len buckets (33→64, 52→64), 132 base64 characters, and kinds 13/14/1059/10050. notes.accuracy: The spec facts hold up: the NIP-01 id-then-sig flow, the NIP-07 extension wall, kind 24133 for NIP-46, and NIP-49's 91-byte layout (1+1+16+24+1+48) with the ncryptsec test vector. Two overreaches: ch4 calls the scrypt output a 'full-strength' key, which depends on the password's entropy, and ch5 draws NIP-49 as 'unsigned in, signed out' traffic even though ncryptsec never signs anything.
notes.depth: Real mechanisms and numbers: the byte-layout diagram, scrypt log_n=16, r=8, p=1, the 32-byte derived key, the scope grant with a refused kind-5 deletion, and the brute-force cost per guess. An expert would find the trade-offs (remote approval via auth_url, offline guessing cost) worth their time.
notes.clarity: Terms are introduced before use (nsec, window.nostr, relay, the bunker URI). But the narration runs at roughly 300-350 wpm, so a newcomer would have little time to absorb each sentence even with clear frames.
notes.story: A clear arc runs from the problem (the key is the identity) through the extension wall, the remote stretch, encryption at rest, and the synthesis. The question 'not can you sign, but will you sign this' is paid off in ch5, and 'Identity you hold, delegated one signature at a time' is a memorable close.
notes.visual: The palette is consistent and most frames carry their idea: the JSON-to-hash flow, the relay diagram, the byte-layout bar, and the scope card with a refused row. Weak spots are tiny labels that overlap the trust-boundary line and node borders, a bunker box that disappears while the narration still refers to it, and translucent end cards that let the scene beneath show through.
notes.sync: Every caption's tile time matches its authored start plus half its length, and the key beats (the key appearing in ch3, the byte layout in ch4, the refused scope in ch5) land on their captions. notes.accuracy: The frames match the captions on the stage: the Biscuit gate, relay circuit, provider table and sidecar stream are all drawn as described. notes.depth: The mechanisms are concrete: AuthFrame handshake, AllowReserve, a gossip fast path before fan-out, and a namespaced tool split from the service name. notes.clarity: Captions are short and each one carries one idea, and MCP is expanded on first use. Biscuit, libp2p, relay and ACL are used without definition, and at the authored durations most captions run well above a newcomer's comfortable pace.
notes.story: The arc is clear: identity, then gate, then discovery, then one call, and each chapter's ending line hands off to the next. The planted question ('one local secret... nothing can trust it yet') is paid off in ch2's 'not a free pass'. The four closing cards share one template, which makes the endings feel repetitive.

I could not hear the audio, so this is judged from the script and durations.

notes.accuracy: Chapter 1 stores only a hash of the bank password, but the extraction service must log in to the bank every day, which needs the real credential or a token. The script never resolves this, so the central mechanism is wrong as stated. Chapter 2 says 'ten categories' while the frames show four bins, and the income template adds to 90%.
notes.depth: The chapters give real mechanisms: a seeded dictionary sized at about 12 MB, a max-heap for crowd overrides with peek in O(1), a template plus stored exceptions, and a MapReduce mapper and reducer with a trade-off panel for each. The credential-handling gap and the thin treatment of retries and rate limits keep it short of expert-grade.
notes.clarity: Each chapter introduces one idea at a time with a plain caption, and the frames match the caption beats. Terms such as hash, queue, heap and map reduce get a short gloss, though some captions pack several clauses into one sentence.
notes.story: The question planted in Chapter 1, 'what happens to each transaction next', is answered in Chapter 2. The December row is set up in Chapter 3 and paid off at the filter, and the closing lines echo Chapter 1's 'speak up before the money runs out'.
notes.visual: Diagrams use a consistent dark palette and stay legible, and the progressive build works. Acme Rent overlaps the funnel edge in Chapter 2 at about 18s, the stat and footnote text in Chapter 1 at 46.75s and the formula text in Chapter 2 is very small, and the closing cards sit over faded ghost diagrams.
notes.sync: Captions and visual beats line up in the frames, but the authored caption lengths are too short for their text: about 290 to 320 words per minute, so the cues cannot carry the narration as timed. Motion and audio were not visible, so this stays provisional.
notes.sound: By word count, the narration implied by the caption timings runs about 270 to 320 wpm, well above the 110-170 target, and the Chapter 1 and 2 captions are the worst. Identifiers such as SQS, API and RabbitMQ appear only on screen, and no pronunciation handling is visible in the script.
notes.curiosity: Each chapter ends on a hook: 'What happens to each transaction next is the interesting part', 'when to tap you on the shoulder', and 'speak up only when a line gets crossed'. The credential question left open in Chapter 1 is a natural draw toward the code.

notes.depth: The LRU walkthrough is concrete: head and tail, O(1) lookup and promotion, the eviction order, and the 270-byte versus 2.7 TB arithmetic. Sharding and TTL get only shallow treatment, with no hot-key, stampede or invalidation trade-offs.

notes.story: The chapter 1 question (keep what, evict what, trust for how long) is answered in order by LRU, then TTL, then sharding. Chapter 3 ends on a sharp hook about a hot query overloading its shard, and the closing card carries it forward.
notes.visual: Most frames are legible and carry the idea. Chapter 2 around t≈57 shows list nodes scattered off the row, one floating at the right edge. notes.accuracy: Ch4 t=45.2 shows a four-node chain (select, score twice, refit, measure residual) while the narration lists six steps, and the calibrate and form-advantages steps never appear. Ch3 shows a '200 / 200' threshold badge from about t=15 while the narration and the plot still say the map is identity until 200 pairs. The 1,174 and 349 GPU-hour figures and the 3.4x ratio agree with each other, but I could not check them against the paper.
notes.depth: The chapters name real mechanisms: the 8x8 batch, a fixed pool of sandboxes, the EWMA weight clip(1+c s², 1, 4), isotonic regression with ten bins, and inverse-variance fusion. Most of these stay at the level of a labelled box, though, and there is little on trade-offs or failure cases beyond the single 'no reordered ranks' note.
notes.clarity: Each chapter introduces one idea per beat, and the visuals stage the sequence well. Several terms are never expanded on screen: EWMA, pool-adjacent-violators, isotonic, and continuous batching. The longer captions in ch1 and ch4 are dense for a newcomer.
notes.story: The 'can the experiment be imagined?' question is planted in ch1 and the arc runs generate, predict, anchor, calibrate, weight, update. The closing card and last line ('every correction remains tied to outcomes the real world actually produced') pay it off well. The ch1 card wording ('can most experiments be graded...') differs slightly from its on-screen title.
notes.visual: The ch4 gradient panels are clipped by the frame edges in several tiles: the left panel is cut off from t=15.2 to 39.2 and the right panel from t=3.2 to 9.2. Many labels are very small or low-contrast, including the scatter points in ch3, the dark-green callout in ch3 at t=27.2, the oval text in ch2, and the anchor-pair labels. The ch1 opening frames sit off-centre with empty space, and a divider line cuts through the batched grid at t=15.2.
notes.sync: Judged from the caption times and frames only, since I cannot see the motion. The main beats mostly land on their captions, such as 1,174 GPU-hours at 51.2 and 'two groups' at 39.2. The ch3 threshold badge and the ch4 four-node chain fall out of step with what is narrated.
notes.sound: Judged from the caption text and authored durations. Several captions run well above 170 wpm, for example ch4 c9 at about 26 words in 5.6 s (roughly 280 wpm), ch1 c9 at about 24 words in 6.4 s (roughly 225 wpm), and ch4 c8 and c11 at about 220 wpm. Numbers are spelled out for the ear, which helps. I lowered this below the 6.5-7.5 band because the density is a clear timing problem in the materials.
notes.curiosity: The 'imagine the outcome, then keep a thin trusted stream' framing and the pairs-of-predicted-and-measured-scores idea both make a viewer want to read the code. The closing 'thin line of ground truth' line leaves a sharp open question.
